- Observe opponents and adapt.

I need to decide on an auction bid for a property.

Short Line is the target. The current bid is $32. I will raise to $33. Then I will mortgage the property for $100. This nets cash because the mortgage value equals half the purchase price.

Winning at $33 nets about $67 cash after mortgaging. I am weighing whether p2 will bid further, since they own no other railroads and a single unmortgaged one would yield little rent.

Mortgaged railroads still count toward the railroad monopoly for rent calculations. If p2 buys Short Line and keeps it unmortgaged, they would have two railroads total and collect only $50 in rent.

The bid will rise in $1 increments up to $99. Paying $99 and mortgaging nets a $1 profit. At $100 the net is zero, and above that the mortgage cannot cover the cost. The goal is to secure liquidity before rolling from Water Works, since p2 holds dangerous properties.

p2 owns an Orange monopoly with four houses each on St. James, Tennessee, and New York. They also own Park Place and Boardwalk with three houses each. Their red properties are Kentucky, Illinois, and Indiana; Indiana is mortgaged, but the other two are unmortgaged and form a complete red monopoly.

I am using my light blue properties as a weapon. p2 has only $225 cash, so overpaying for Short Line would drain their liquidity and leave them vulnerable to my heavy light blue rents. I am recalling the exact rent values for Oriental Avenue with four houses.
